contributions.item_title_en: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
contributions.text_english: Minister, Wales needs both renewable energy and secure domestic food production. Welsh planning policy already gives considerable weight to protecting our best and most versatile agricultural land. Can you explain how the protection works alongside the Government's drive for renewable energy, so that we increase green generation without unnecessarily losing our most productive farmland?

contributions.item_title_en: 1. Questions to the Trefnydd, Chief Whip and Cabinet Minister for Culture and Sport
contributions.text_english: People are rightly concerned as to why valued libraries and leisure facilities have been allowed to disappear. Will the Cabinet Minister work with councils and Sport Wales to ensure that, before any facilities are closed and lost forever, the community is given the evidence, available alternatives and genuine opportunity to retain them through community ownership or genuine like-for-like replacement provision?

contributions.item_title_en: 10. Short Debate: Improving access to local economic opportunities in Casnewydd Islwyn
contributions.text_english:
Diolch. I'm giving a minute to Jayne Bryant and Peredur Griffiths.

I'm grateful for the opportunity to bring forward this short debate on improving access to local economic opportunities in Casnewydd Islwyn. Economic opportunity is not only about whether jobs, courses, schemes or support exist somewhere in the system; it is about whether people can see those opportunities, reach them and use them. People in Casnewydd Islwyn want decent work. They want young people to have a future close to home. They want local businesses to succeed. This depends on the Welsh Government, local government, colleges, employers and community groups working together. But Government has a role in making the system easier to understand and easier to access. This is the argument of this debate.

If a young person cannot see the links between what they study and the work available to them, ambition starts to look like something you have to leave the area to find. We should want people here to see a future in Wales and understand the route to it. If an adult wants to retrain or move into better work, this starting point should not depend on already knowing how the system works. If a local employer wants to expand, take on apprentices or invest in a site, they should know where to go, what support exists and who is responsible. They should not have to chase different parts of the public sector to find out.

Economic development sounds abstract. Its impact is not. A secure job changes a household. A training route gives someone confidence. An apprenticeship changes what a family believes is possible. That is why access to opportunities should be treated as a delivery test. Can people see what is available? Can they reach it? Can they use it?

I want to ask the Welsh Government three things. First, how will you make the local economy offer—skills, training, apprenticeships, employment support and growth sector routes—more visible in constituencies such as Casnewydd Islwyn? Second, how will you strengthen the links between education, skills and local employers so people understand what skills are needed and how to move from one stage to the next? Third, how will you make it easier for local employers to engage with the public sector when they want to grow, invest and create jobs?

This debate is about access. Casnewydd Islwyn has ambition, capable businesses and communities that want to see delivery. The task is to make the route into opportunities clear. This is the spirit in which I bring this debate forward. Thank you.

contributions.item_title_en: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
contributions.text_english:
Before I ask my supplementary, I declare my registered interest as a former employee of Abercarn rugby club. Abercarn welfare ground shows the real impact that flooding and sewerage contamination has on a community. The ground supports rugby, football and cricket. Sewage has surfaced on the field and pitches have sat unusable for weeks at a time, disrupting local sports and raising clear public health and environmental concerns. The wider issue is ageing sewerage infrastructure, polluted waterways, flood risk and contaminated land, with community facilities left to carry the consequences when systems fail.

What discussions is the Cabinet Secretary having with Dŵr Cymru Welsh Water, National Resources Wales, Caerphilly County Borough Council and the UK Government to bring forward plans with clear deadlines for Abercarn welfare ground, covering testing, clean-up, public health advice and long-term sewerage and drainage works, and what is the Welsh Government doing to secure the powers, regulation and resources needed to stop sewage contamination and flooding from damaging community facilities in the future?

contributions.item_title_en: 3. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning
contributions.text_english: Over the past year, private rents in Newport have risen by almost 20 per cent, and, at the same time, in almost 70 per cent of areas across Wales, Shelter Cymru have found that there are no properties advertised for rent within the local housing allowance rate. This gap between housing costs and support levels is leaving many households with no viable option, contributing directly to rising homelessness and increasing reliance on temporary accommodation. Given the clear pressures this is placing on local authorities and the long-term financial constraints that temporary accommodation creates for budgets, beyond increasing social housing supply, what work is being undertaken to support councils in moving towards a more phased planned reduction in reliance on temporary accommodation, and to provide the funding stability needed to manage the transition effectively?
